blogs.title: From Ciminelli to Kousisis: The Fifth Circuit Rehabilitates Fraudulent-Inducement in Pump-and-Dump Prosecutions
blogs.description: Explains how the panel distinguishes the now-rejected right-to-control theory from the still-viable fraudulent-inducement theory, using Kousisis to hold that inducing followers to part with money for securities via lies states a §1348 offense. Discusses the opinion’s framing of “money or property” and what it signals for DOJ charging decisions in market-manipulation cases.

blogs.title: No Net Loss Needed: Profit Motive as Proof of Fraudulent Intent Under §1348
blogs.description: Analyzes the court’s embrace of Kousisis’s holding that the fraud statutes do not require proof of victim net pecuniary loss. Evaluates the panel’s reasoning that victims receiving market-value securities does not defeat criminal liability, and considers how this reshapes defense theories, jury instructions on intent, and the evidentiary focus at trial.

blogs.title: Influencers, Hype, and Securities Fraud: When Online Touting Crosses the Line
blogs.description: Uses the case’s allegations—misstatements about trading positions and price potential—to explore doctrinal boundaries between protected opinion/puffery and actionable falsehoods in criminal securities fraud. Considers First Amendment tensions, ‘scalping’ analogies, and how covert selling and coordination can turn stock-picking content into a prosecutable scheme.

blogs.title: Why Charge §1348? The Government’s Criminal Route Around Civil 10b-5 Doctrines
blogs.description: Compares §1348’s mail/wire-fraud-derived elements with classic Rule 10b-5 concepts, highlighting what prosecutors gain (no reliance element; focus on scheme and intent to obtain money) and potential defense angles. Examines the interplay with §1349 conspiracy and aiding-and-abetting liability for coordinated social-media trading campaigns.

blogs.title: Drafting Indictments After Kousisis: What the Fifth Circuit Expects in Market-Manipulation Cases
blogs.description: Dissects the opinion’s sufficiency analysis: alleging a material deception, the object of obtaining victims’ money via induced purchases, and intent to deceive and cause cognizable harm. Offers takeaways on the level of detail needed to satisfy notice and double-jeopardy functions without pleading loss or reliance.

blogs.title: Ciminelli Overread? The Fifth Circuit Cabins Right-to-Control While Preserving Traditional Fraud
blogs.description: Critiques the district court’s dismissal and explains the appellate correction: Ciminelli bars treating ‘valuable economic information’ as property, but does not disable fraudulent-inducement theories that target victims’ money. Situates the opinion within a broader post-Ciminelli trend of limiting, not expanding, the decision’s reach.

blogs.title: Sentencing and Restitution After a Social-Media Pump-and-Dump: The Coming Fights
blogs.description: Forecasts disputes likely to follow a conviction: calculating loss and restitution where victims bought at ‘market’ but under artificial inflation, intended loss vs. actual loss, and foreseeability. Assesses how the court’s “fraud is complete upon induced deprivation” language may influence Guidelines arguments and causation showings.

blogs.title: Coordinated Online Trading and the Future of Market-Manipulation Enforcement
blogs.description: Places the case in the larger enforcement arc targeting influencer-driven schemes. Discusses how coordination plus misrepresentation fits §1348’s ‘scheme to defraud’ model, potential chilling effects on retail-trading communities, and what the decision portends for parallel SEC actions and criminal prosecutions nationwide.
